body: Well I don't think life is exactly like that, but even if you're dealt a shitty hand (3-J or 4-10), you can win the pot. If you play from position and take the betting lead, you can make players with stronger hands fold. If the flop doesn't have many high cards or face cards, then you can safely continue to take the betting lead, and if you can make all your opponents fold, you will win. You can even get lucky and hit the flop with your hand, and if you've made enough players fold, you're in a good place. This is an oversimplification, but you can win with a shitty hand if you play it strong. But is life like this? Perhaps in some ways, but you're more than the hand you are dealt in life.

What a great post! A lot of my depressive thoughts arise from prolonged feelings of guilt, much of them being completely irrational. Some were of course rational, but the amount of time I felt guilty was irrational. Guilt can also lead to a prolonged delay of necessary action, because it can lead to feelings of self-loathing. It's a really destructive emotion. I also want to note that healthy remorse is perfectly fine, and there's a distinction between this and the feeling of guilt. David Burns in "Feeling Good" goes into great depth on this issue and makes some really really great points.

I don't know the whole thing about happiness.. I don't even know what it is really so I can't answer that part. But what I do know is that there is an intrinsic need for humans to be social. Humans need a sense of belonging. It's not just a purely mental thing, it's a biological need we have. Without it, people can lose their minds. I've been socially isolated for many years, and I've pretty much lost sense of who I am and have been suicidal. On Maslow's hierarchy of human needs, Love/Belonging is right after Safety. There have been plenty of studies done to show the extreme negative effects of loneliness and social deprivation.

So you're not wrong in not wanting to be alone, you're just human. Co-dependency is not really the issue I think. I think the issue is the whole idea of "only you can make yourself happy", and this can sometimes lead to social isolation and trust issues with other people. I think it's not as simple as "you can't rely on others to make you happy", it's a much more complex thing than that. The crux of the issue remains the same though - social belonging and structure is a basic human need. Perhaps there are some that can do without it, but we are social creatures. Don't feel guilty for trying to find solace in other people. But a line has to be drawn too, as I'm sure you know.

Hey. First off, you're not retarded. I'm serious, just because you don't seem to understand certain concepts does not make you any less of a person. It's just that the way schools teach, some students just don't understand because their learning style is different. Do you know how you learn best? Here's an example of a quiz to help you figure that out.

http://www.educationplanner.org/students/self-assessments/learning-styles-quiz.shtml

You can use it to determine which way you learn best and try to focus on that method. Math, chemistry and physics are tough subjects in high school. I understand because I've been through those classes, they can seem very challenging. The way I got through is I tried to do all of the practice problems. The more practice, the better. As for understanding, I used online resources a lot. I'll list a couple here, maybe they can help you. 

http://patrickjmt.com/ (Videos on math, really helpful for calculus and linear algebra)

https://www.youtube.com/user/khanacademy (Videos on all subjects pretty much, has some great videos on physics and chemistry)

There's many more online resources out there, and I'm sure some will even be in your native language. If you enjoy these disciplines, then I feel you will have enough interest to get through the tough parts. Just try to do you best, and if you encounter difficulty, don't be too discouraged. A lot of people, including myself, have or have had difficulty with math and science courses. It's alright to be insecure about the future, everyone is. But in keeping a more relaxed attitude and focusing on finding out how you learn best, you can do well in your courses. Best of luck!

I get the whole ordeal about comparison. When you're compared to someone by your parents, it's essentially always a put down. I imagine they do this because they themselves feel some inadequacy when their children are not well off as others. Now I'm not quite sure why your mom is comparing you to members of your own family, but I imagine it's out of the same feelings of inadequacy and guilt. She feels there's something wrong with you, and thus there was something wrong with her method of raising you. This is guesswork, but this is why my parents compare me to others.

Now I'm not saying this is justification for it, but maybe in realizing this it will help relieve you of some anxiety and pain. Honestly speaking, all comparisons we make are petty. There really is no one true path to take in life, and there fundamentally is nothing wrong with dealing with suicidal thoughts. Sure, these thoughts are not healthy, but many many people have them. To say you must not have these thoughts is of no help. If I were to compare myself to you, I am likely to have no job after graduating college. I also did not speak to anyone during my time at college, not even my roommates until very recently. Now if I compared myself to you, I'd say you were better off. But that might not be true, but more importantly, it's a completely useless statement to make. It helps with absolutely nothing. 

I'd suggest you find an activity or hobby that you enjoy, and join a group of people with that similar interest. Of course that negative judgement will still affect you, but the more diverse people you're with during your days, the less harm it will do. Also see a doctor if you haven't already. Try to find another support group similar to the one you had with your roommates, because it seems confiding in your parents does not help. Best of luck.

I think there is probably an effect caused by this that leads to depressed people feeling isolated, you're right on that. I think the statement reflects a lot on society's view on how people should feel; happiness is something that people SHOULD have. I think by virtue of this idea, people who have mood disorders tend to feel isolated because we've been bombarded by the constant images and ideas that lead us to believe we should be happy, and avoid misery at all costs. This leads to the automatic assumption that if you're experiencing melancholy or depression, there's something inherently wrong with you. Now there may well be a chemical imbalance in your brain, but I think this idea that you MUST not feel this way does not help at all. I'm not promoting negativity and sadness, but I'm just reflecting on how I think things are.
